title: Hera Nears Asteroid Pair to Examine NASA DART Impact Damage, Gizmodo Reports
body:
A joint mission between NASA and the European Space Agency is set to reach the binary asteroid system Didymos in November, where it will conduct the first close‑up inspection of the impact scar left by the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART). The Hera spacecraft, launched in 2023, will rendezvous with both the primary body Didymos and its moonlet Dimorphos, positioning itself to study the crater, debris field and any subtle changes in the bodies’ orbits that resulted from DART’s kinetic‑impact experiment last year.

The DART mission, which deliberately slammed a 0.6‑tonne probe into Dimorphos in September 2022, was the world’s inaugural test of a planetary‑defence technique that could one day be used to avert a catastrophic asteroid strike on Earth. By measuring the resulting shift in Dimorphos’s orbital period around Didymos, scientists confirmed that a high‑speed impact can indeed alter an asteroid’s trajectory. However, the precise physics of the impact—how much material was ejected, the crater’s depth, the momentum transferred to the target, and the long‑term stability of the binary system—remain largely unknown. Hera’s suite of cameras, spectrometers, and a radio science experiment will fill those gaps, providing the first direct observations of a man‑made crater on an asteroid.

The mission’s scientific payload is tailored for a detailed forensic analysis. High‑resolution imaging will map the crater’s morphology at a scale of centimeters, while a thermal infrared spectrometer will assess the composition of the exposed subsurface material. A laser altimeter will generate a three‑dimensional model of both bodies, enabling precise calculations of mass loss and density changes. In addition, Hera will deploy a small CubeSat, called Juventas, to fly closer to the impact site and capture data that the larger spacecraft cannot. Together, these instruments will quantify the momentum enhancement factor (β), a key parameter that describes how much additional thrust is generated by the ejecta plume beyond the kinetic energy of the impactor itself.

Beyond the immediate scientific payoff, Hera’s findings will inform the design of future deflection missions. Current planetary‑defence strategies rely on computer models that extrapolate laboratory experiments to asteroid scales, but real‑world data are scarce. By comparing the observed crater and ejecta distribution with pre‑impact simulations, researchers can refine the models that predict how different asteroid compositions and structures respond to kinetic impacts. This knowledge will be critical if humanity ever needs to divert a larger, potentially hazardous object on a collision course with Earth.

The mission also underscores the growing collaboration between international space agencies in addressing planetary‑defence challenges. While NASA provided the DART impactor, ESA contributed the Hera spacecraft and its scientific instruments, and both agencies share data with the broader scientific community. The partnership demonstrates a unified approach to a problem that transcends national borders, reinforcing the notion that safeguarding the planet is a collective responsibility.

As Hera approaches the Didymos system later this year, anticipation builds within the planetary‑science community. The data returned will not only validate the efficacy of kinetic‑impact deflection but also reveal any unforeseen consequences—such as changes in the binary’s mutual orbit or the creation of secondary fragments—that could affect future mitigation strategies. In the months and years ahead, the insights gained from Hera’s close‑up examination will shape the next generation of asteroid‑defence missions, bringing humanity a step closer to mastering the art of protecting Earth from extraterrestrial threats.
